title: Introduction to Graph Theory: A Computer Science Perspective
beats: Simplest definition: a graph is a network of relationships; circles are components, lines are relations; then name them vertices/edges
Roadmap: why care, definitions, terminology, representations, open problems
Why care: graphs show up everywhere; maps with intersections as vertices
Social network friend recommendation as graph question
Sudoku as an unexpected graph: coloring with row, column, box constraints
Formal definition: sets V and E, edge as vertex pair, with concrete example
Terminology: neighbors, degree, path, path length, cycle, connectivity (three senses), connected component, each with a pictured example
Types: undirected, directed, cyclic/acyclic, weighted, trees with three properties
Pause to check tree properties; calls verifying them satisfying
How would a computer store this graph?
Three representations: adjacency matrix, edge set, adjacency list
Pick adjacency list because real graphs are sparse; social network memory argument
Open problems: connectivity, shortest path, cycle detection, coloring, Eulerian-style path
Path through every vertex once has no efficient known algorithm; P vs NP hint with joke about awards

metrics.examples: 3 motivating applications (maps, social, Sudoku), then one running graph for terms plus new small pictured graphs for each term; no growth in difficulty
metrics.ending: recap then tease of future algorithm videos; hard Hamiltonian-path surprise sits just before

theory: This is a vocabulary-and-motivation video: it buys attention by showing graphs hidden in familiar things, then gives the minimum shared language for later algorithm videos. It stays out of discovery and practice, trading depth for breadth. The one strong teaching choice is stating why the adjacency list wins, tying a data-structure choice to a real-world fact (sparsity).
velocity: Opening scene builder: a familiar map or friend network that morphs into nodes and edges on screen
Orchestrator: for vocabulary-heavy beats, pair each new term with a highlighted piece of the same running graph and cap new terms per minute
Voice: justify each tool choice with a real-world constraint (sparse graphs) as a short 'why this one' beat
Learner model: mark terms as introduced and insert recall checks, as this video has none
Evals: flag beats that introduce more than ~3 new terms without an example or pause
quote: for this reason in future videos we will primarily use adjacency lists
